patient.history_present_illness: A 58-year-old man with known alcoholic cirrhosis was brought to the emergency department by his neighbor after being found confused and combative at home. According to the neighbor, the patient had been complaining of dark, tarry stools for approximately 24 hours prior to presentation. He was found sitting in a chair, unable to recognize his neighbor and shouting incoherently. Over the past few days, the patient had reportedly stopped eating, was not taking his lactulose as prescribed, and had continued drinking alcohol. His neighbor noted that his abdomen appeared more distended than usual. He had no known history of seizures or head trauma. On arrival to the ED, the patient was oriented only to his name, was agitated and pulling at IV lines, and could not provide a coherent history. He smelled strongly of alcohol. His skin was visibly jaundiced. He was tachycardic and hypotensive on arrival. Blood was noted on rectal exam, confirming active lower GI blood loss. No focal neurological deficits were identified on initial assessment, and there was no evidence of meningismus. The patient's daughter, reached by phone, confirmed he had a history of hepatic encephalopathy once before, two years ago following a GI bleed, which resolved with lactulose and rifaximin. She reported he had been increasingly confused over the past 48 hours and had refused to go to the hospital until his neighbor forced the issue today.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, Grade 3, acute-on-chronic, with multiple precipitants (GI hemorrhage, hypokalemia, alcohol intoxication, lactulose non-compliance)

differential.key_features: Alcoholism is present but MRI shows no periaqueductal/mammillary T2 signal; classic triad incomplete; thiamine low but HE pattern dominates; give thiamine empirically
BAL 142 mg/dL contributes to altered mental status but does not explain hyperammonemia (187 umol/L) or triphasic waves on EEG; alcohol is co-precipitant for HE
Creatinine only 1.4 mg/dL; BUN elevated predominantly from GI protein load; no history of renal failure; does not explain hyperammonemia
No fever, no meningismus, CT normal, CSF not indicated in this presentation; triphasic waves on EEG not typical of CNS infection
EEG shows triphasic waves without true epileptiform activity; benzodiazepine challenge negative; no ictal evolution; excluded by cEEG

tool_parameters.query: hepatic encephalopathy management acute GI hemorrhage lactulose rifaximin

critical_actions: Administer IV thiamine BEFORE dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Initiate lactulose (30mL q2h) and rifaximin (550mg BID) for ammonia reduction
CT head to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before attributing AMS to HE
Perform EEG to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Urgent GI consultation for upper GI hemorrhage (likely variceal)
Correct coagulopathy with FFP for active bleeding (INR 2.8)
Correct hypokalemia (precipitant for HE) with IV potassium
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT give dextrose before thiamine in an alcoholic patient
Do NOT use benzodiazepines (sedatives) in active hepatic encephalopathy — worsens encephalopathy
Do NOT give NSAIDs (worsen renal function, GI bleeding risk in cirrhosis)
Do NOT use protein restriction — modern guidelines recommend adequate protein intake even in HE
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture without first excluding coagulopathy (INR 2.8 — high hemorrhage risk)
Do NOT use morphine or opioids for agitation (hepatically metabolized; worsen encephalopathy)
Do NOT rapidly correct hyponatremia (osmotic demyelination risk)
key_reasoning_points: Markedly elevated ammonia (187 umol/L) with classic triphasic waves on EEG in a patient with known cirrhosis is highly characteristic of hepatic encephalopathy
Multiple identified precipitants: GI hemorrhage (BUN 64 mg/dL with BUN:Cr >30:1, Hgb 8.1), lactulose non-compliance, alcohol intoxication (BAL 142), hypokalemia
CT head is normal — structural cause excluded; diagnosis is metabolic
EEG triphasic waves at 1.5-2.5 Hz are characteristic of HE but not pathognomonic; NCSE must be excluded (benzodiazepine challenge negative)
Thiamine replacement before glucose is mandatory in any alcoholic presenting with encephalopathy
AST:ALT ratio >2:1 with markedly elevated GGT suggests alcoholic hepatitis superimposed on cirrhosis
MELD 26 with recurrent HE and GI hemorrhage warrants transplant evaluation after sobriety establishment
Hyponatremia (Na 128) is dilutional in cirrhosis — cautious fluid management needed; do NOT rapidly correct
Hypoglycemia (glucose 61 mg/dL) from impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis is a contributing factor to AMS

red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may attribute entire AMS to acute alcohol intoxication and not pursue workup for HE
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Alcohol intoxication is a co-precipitant but cannot explain ammonia 187 umol/L or EEG triphasic waves; HE must be treated simultaneously

red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may suspect uremic encephalopathy as primary cause
